results.question: Is there a waiting period before I can get the general social security benefit?
results.answer:
Yes, there is usually a waiting period (omavastuuaika) of 7 working days before you can receive the general social security benefit [S2]. 

You must be registered as an unemployed jobseeker with the employment services for at least 7 working days to complete this waiting period [S2]. If you work part-time, your waiting period is calculated by deducting your worked hours from the maximum working hours in your collective agreement until they amount to 7 full working days [S2]. 

However, you do not need to complete a new waiting period if you transition directly from earnings-related unemployment allowance to the general social security benefit [S2][S5].

results.question: I have no vocational qualification. Do I have to wait longer before I get the general social security benefit?
results.answer:
If you do not have a vocational qualification or a higher education degree, you generally must complete a qualifying period (odotusaika) before you can receive the general social security benefit [S1][S4]. Upper secondary school and the matriculation examination do not count as vocational qualifications [S1][S4]. 

The maximum length of this qualifying period is 21 weeks, which is about 5 months [S3][S8]. Additionally, if you are under 25, you must apply for admission to at least two study programmes starting in the autumn term to qualify for the benefit [S4][S8].

results.question: How does part-time work affect my general social security benefit?
results.answer:
You can still receive the general social security benefit while working part-time [S2]. 

Your earnings will reduce the amount of your benefit, resulting in an adjusted general social security benefit [S5]. As a basic rule, the benefit is reduced by 50 cents for every euro you earn in wages or salary [S8]. The income affects the benefit during the specific payment period in which the wages are actually paid to you, regardless of when you earned them [S1].

results.question: Can income other than wages reduce my general social security benefit?
results.answer:
Yes, income other than wages or salary can reduce your general social security benefit because the benefit is means-tested [S1][S3]. 

Other income that can reduce your benefit includes capital income, informal care allowances, partial early old-age pensions, compensations for family caregivers, and copyright royalties [S3]. Kela takes these types of income into account in the means test [S2]. 

You can have up to EUR 311 per month in capital income or other non-wage income without it affecting your benefit [S4]. If you exceed this EUR 311 limit, 50% of the amount exceeding the limit will be deducted from your general social security benefit [S4]. However, if you participate in employment-promoting services, non-wage income will not reduce your benefit [S4].

results.question: Can I still apply for labour market subsidy?
results.answer:
